name: Camera Angles
description: Camera height and tilt relative to the subjects. Entries explain the visible viewpoint without moving subjects or their physical supports.
entries: chest-height front angle: the view meets the subjects below eye level while keeping the horizon level
shoulder-height angle: the view looks horizontally just below the subjects' eyes
seated eye-level angle: the view meets seated subjects at their eye height rather than looking down from standing height
table-height angle: the view looks across the working surface with the subjects rising beyond it
stair-level angle: the view looks horizontally from an existing step toward subjects on another level
balcony angle: the view looks downward from the edge of an elevated gallery
upward architectural angle: the view rises past the subjects toward the structure overhead
shallow downward angle: the view looks slightly down, keeping faces and nearby hand placement visible
steep upward angle: the view looks sharply up from near the base of the main subjects
ceiling-corner angle: the view looks diagonally across the space from a high corner
waterline angle: the view sits just above the water surface and looks horizontally toward the subjects
bank-level angle: the view looks down from a raised shore toward subjects on lower ground
low angle: the view looks upward from below the main subjects, showing their undersides and the space above them
high angle: the view looks downward from above the main subjects, showing their upper surfaces and the ground around them
Dutch angle: the view is rolled sideways so the horizon is diagonal, without tilting the subjects' physical supports
eye-level angle: the view meets the main subjects at their eye height, without looking up or down at them
ground-level angle: the view looks across the ground from beside the subjects' feet or bases, with foreground surfaces prominent
overhead angle: the view looks straight down onto the main subjects and the layout around them
waist-level angle: the view looks horizontally across the subjects at the height of their middle, keeping vertical supports upright
raised oblique angle: the view looks diagonally down from one side, revealing both the fronts and upper surfaces of the main subjects
